notes.title: Start here: a support-ticket hub and its verified findings
notes.body:
This pack uses Support Hub, a Next.js + Prisma app where support agents, leads and managers work customer tickets, and customers use a portal. Tickets move between statuses, get reassigned, and carry SLA deadlines (first response, resolution).

The docs come in two folders:

- `docs/learning/`: `guided-reading-path.md` walks the code file by file; `concepts-demonstrated.md` explains each pattern with a Mechanism, a Limit and a Check; `testing-rationale.md` lists the checks C1-C10.
- `docs/architecture/`: `README.md` ends with thirteen verified findings (F1-F13), and `auth-and-permissions.md` has the role matrix and a five-rung Goal/Check ladder.

Suggested order: the guided reading path (steps 1-5 at least), then `concepts-demonstrated.md` from "Service layer" onwards, then `auth-and-permissions.md`, then the findings in `docs/architecture/README.md`. Most quizzes are about what the code *really* does where it differs from the design, so keep `src/services/ticket-service.ts` open and check every line number the docs give.

excerpts.quote: The entries above say where to look. This section says what the code actually does, where it stops, and how to confirm you understood it.
The UI is not the source of truth for permissions or transitions; it only surfaces the server-owned workflows.

notes.title: Thin routes, services that own the rules
notes.body:
The intended design: a route handler in `src/app/api/**` reads the session, validates the body with Zod, and hands over to a service function. The service checks permissions with the `assert*` helpers from `src/lib/permissions/policies.ts`, loads the ticket, and does its writes in one `prisma.$transaction`. Errors are turned into HTTP responses in one place, `withRouteErrorHandling`.

When you trace a quiz scenario, follow it through four questions:

1. Which route and which service function does the request hit?
2. Which permission helper (if any) runs, and which error does it throw?
3. Does the service go through the status transition table, or write `status` directly?
4. What does `withRouteErrorHandling` turn the error into?

The "Limit" lines in `concepts-demonstrated.md` tell you where each of these steps is weaker than it looks.

excerpts.quote: Route handlers stay small on purpose; they should not start owning workflow conditions or permission branches.
boolean role predicates plus `assert*` wrappers in `src/lib/permissions/policies.ts`, called at the top of each service function.

readMore.why: How one request travels from route to response, including the non-permission failures.

notes.title: How an SLA state is computed
notes.body:
Each ticket has deadlines computed from its creation time. On every write, the service recomputes an SLA *state* for each deadline with `getSlaState` in `src/lib/utils/dates.ts`. The possible states are MET, PAUSED, BREACHED, AT_RISK and HEALTHY.

`getSlaState` is a short chain of `if` statements. When more than one condition could be true at once, the order of the checks decides the answer, so write that order down before anything else.

It also relies on two `date-fns` helpers, `isAfter` and `differenceInMinutes`. Look both up in the date-fns documentation and note exactly how each behaves at the edges: two equal times, and a gap that is not a whole number of minutes.

Then read `evaluateSlaTracking` in `src/services/sla-service.ts` (lines 67-100) and trace what happens to a deadline, and to the time spent paused, when a ticket is paused and later resumes.

excerpts.quote: export const getSlaState = ( dueAt: Date, actualAt: Date | null, now: Date, thresholdMinutes: number, isPaused: boolean, ): SlaState => {
deadlines are `createdAt + N minutes` (`src/services/sla-service.ts:37-38`)

notes.title: Internal is not the same as allowed to write
notes.body:
**Key: 403 with "Only internal support staff can add internal notes."**

`addInternalNote` starts with `assertCanAddInternalNote(session)`. That helper tests `canModifyTickets`, which is true only for `SUPPORT_AGENT`, `SUPPORT_LEAD` and `SUPPORT_MANAGER`. The observer fails it, and `forbidden(...)` gives a 403. The message is a little ironic: `isInternalUser` does count the observer as internal, but writing needs `canModifyTickets`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *200*: being internal lets an observer read notes, not write them.
- *409*: this helper uses `forbidden`, not `conflict`.
- *404*: the permission check runs before the ticket is loaded.

excerpts.quote: if (!canModifyTickets(session.role)) { throw forbidden("Only internal support staff can add internal notes.");

readMore.why: Internal roles versus roles that may modify tickets.

notes.title: Two email checks that disagree about letter case
notes.body:
**Key: the detail page opens, but the ticket is missing from their list.**

There are two ownership checks for portal users. The detail check in `policies.ts` lowercases both emails before comparing, so "Pat@Example.com" matches "pat@example.com" and the page opens. The list query in `ticket-repository.ts` filters with `requester: { email: visibility.requesterEmail }`, an exact match in the database, so the ticket is left out of the list. The same user sees the ticket in one place and not the other.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Both list and detail*: the list query is case-sensitive.
- *List but 403 on detail*: it is the other way round.
- *Nowhere*: the detail check does match.

excerpts.quote: session.role === "CUSTOMER_PORTAL" && session.email.toLowerCase() === ticket.requester.email.toLowerCase()
...(visibility?.requesterEmail ? { requester: { email: visibility.requesterEmail, }, }
detail compares case-insensitively, list compares exactly (`policies.ts:48` vs `ticket-repository.ts:103-109`)

notes.title: Escalation writes the status directly
notes.body:
**Key: a transition check and the status-history row for the change.**

`escalateTicket` updates the ticket with `status: ticket.status === "CLOSED" ? ticket.status : "ESCALATED"`. It never calls `assertValidStatusTransition` (so PENDING → ESCALATED is not checked against the table) and never calls `createStatusHistory` (so the timeline shows an escalation but no status change). Finding F7 adds that SLA tracking is not re-evaluated, so a PENDING ticket stays paused.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Nothing, it goes through changeTicketStatus*: it does not; only `changeTicketStatus` uses the table.
- *The status change stays PENDING*: the update does set ESCALATED.
- *No audit row*: every mutating workflow writes an AuditLog row in its transaction; what is missing is the *status history*.

excerpts.quote: await repository.updateTicket(ticket.id, { isEscalated: true, escalatedAt: ticket.escalatedAt ?? new Date(), status: ticket.status === "CLOSED" ? ticket.status : "ESCALATED", });
but never calls `assertValidStatusTransition()` or `createStatusHistory()`. The ticket timeline therefore shows an escalation but no status change.

notes.body:
**Key: "you can name the line that would need to change (`session.ts:30`) and what it would do instead (verify a signature, or look up a server-side session row)."**

This is a goal-check question: the Goal/Check ladder at the end of `auth-and-permissions.md` pairs five goals with five checks, and the wrong choices are the checks of the other rungs.

Rung 1's goal is to explain why `httpOnly` does not make the session trustworthy. `httpOnly` stops page scripts from reading the cookie, but the user can still edit it, and `readSession` trusts whatever JSON it finds on line 30. Showing you understand means naming that line and the two real fixes: check a signature, or keep the session on the server.

Why the others do not fit:
- *List both reassignment paths*: rung 2.
- *`forbidden()` on lines 283 and 404*: rung 5, the 409 bug.
- *`dashboard: null` for agents*: rung 4, the bootstrap fix.

notes.title: Paused SLA time is never credited
notes.body:
**Key: BREACHED, because the pause is only a label and no time is credited.**

When the ticket resumes, `evaluateSlaTracking` sets `pausedAt` to `null` (line 78) and copies `accumulatedPauseMs` through unchanged (line 83). No code anywhere adds the paused minutes to it or moves the due date. So the deadline is still 13:00. At 14:00 the ticket is no longer paused, `now` is after the deadline, and `getSlaState` returns BREACHED. Finding F4 reproduces exactly this case.

Why the others are wrong:
- *HEALTHY, deadline pushed to 14:40*: that would need code that credits pause time; there is none.
- *Still PAUSED*: `shouldPause` is false after resume, so `isPaused` is false.
- *AT_RISK*: the deadline is in the past, so the BREACHED check comes first.

excerpts.quote: const pausedAt = shouldPause ? input.existing.pausedAt ?? input.now : null; return { isPaused: shouldPause, pausedAt, accumulatedPauseMs: input.existing.accumulatedPauseMs,
Nothing in `src/` ever adds to `accumulatedPauseMs`, and no code moves a due date after creation.

notes.title: At the deadline and at 15m59s, both are AT_RISK
notes.body:
**Key: AT_RISK both times, as neither moment is past the deadline yet.**

Exactly at the deadline, `isAfter(now, dueAt)` compares two equal times. `isAfter` is strict, so it is false and BREACHED is skipped. `differenceInMinutes` is 0, and 0 <= 15, so AT_RISK. At 15 minutes 59 seconds before, `isAfter` is false again. `differenceInMinutes` counts whole minutes and drops the 59 seconds, giving 15, and 15 <= 15, so AT_RISK.

Why the others are wrong:
- *HEALTHY at 15m59s*: that would need rounding up to 16; the function truncates.
- *BREACHED at the due instant*: strict `isAfter` is false at equality.
- *Both*: the same two mistakes combined.

excerpts.quote: if (isAfter(now, dueAt)) { return "BREACHED"; } const remainingMinutes = differenceInMinutes(dueAt, now); return remainingMinutes <= thresholdMinutes ? "AT_RISK" : "HEALTHY";
Exactly at the deadline the state is `AT_RISK`, not `BREACHED`, because `isAfter` is strict (check C6).

notes.title: A late first response still counts as MET
notes.body:
**Key: MET, because actualAt short-circuits before dueAt is compared.**

The first line of `getSlaState` is `if (actualAt) return "MET"`. As soon as a response exists, the function returns MET without ever comparing the response time with the deadline. Five hours late or five minutes early, the result is the same. Finding F5 notes the effect: late responses disappear from every BREACHED counter on the dashboard.

Why the others are wrong:
- *BREACHED, actualAt is later than dueAt*: the function never compares those two.
- *PAUSED for review*: there is no review step; PAUSED is only reached when there is no response.
- *AT_RISK until acknowledged*: no acknowledgement exists in the code.

excerpts.quote: if (actualAt) { return "MET"; }
`getSlaState()` returns `MET` as soon as `actualAt` is set, before comparing it to `dueAt`

notes.title: A customer reply forces WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER, even from RESOLVED
notes.body:
**Key: WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER, an edge that the transition table rejects.**

In `addPublicReply`, `nextStatus` is `"WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER"` whenever the author's role is `CUSTOMER_PORTAL`, whatever the current status. The code does not call `assertValidStatusTransition`, so nothing checks the move. From RESOLVED that produces RESOLVED → WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER, which the real transition table rejects (check C2). The name is also backwards: after the customer has replied, support is the one who must act.

Why the others are wrong:
- *OPEN via the reopen edge*: the code never picks OPEN for a customer author.
- *Refused with 409*: there is no check that could refuse it.
- *Stays RESOLVED*: `nextStatus` is written to the ticket.

excerpts.quote: const nextStatus = session.role === "CUSTOMER_PORTAL" ? "WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER" : ticket.status === "NEW" ? "OPEN" : ticket.status;
Run against the real transition table, a reply on a `RESOLVED` ticket produces `RESOLVED -> WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER`, which the table rejects (check C2).

notes.title: Malformed JSON is a 500; an empty object is a 400
notes.body:
**Key: 500 for `{`, a SyntaxError, and 400 for `{}`, a ZodError from parseJson.**

`parseJson` does two steps: `await request.json()`, then `schema.parse(json)`. The body `{` is not valid JSON, so the first step throws a `SyntaxError`. Only `ZodError` is mapped to 400; anything else falls through to 500. The body `{}` is valid JSON, so Zod runs and fails because required create fields are missing: a `ZodError`, so 400 VALIDATION_ERROR.

Why the others are wrong:
- *400 for both*: `request.json()` fails before Zod can run.
- *201 for `{}`*: the create schema has required fields.
- *500 for both*: the route does handle errors, through `withRouteErrorHandling`.

excerpts.quote: export const parseJson = async <T>(request: Request, schema: ZodSchema<T>) => { const json = await request.json(); return schema.parse(json); };
a body that is not JSON throws before Zod runs and becomes `500`.

notes.title: A cookie that does not parse is no session
notes.body:
**Key: 401, since an unparsable cookie reads as no session at all.**

`readSession` gets the cookie value and runs `JSON.parse(raw)` inside `try`; the `catch` returns `null`. The notes route calls `requireRouteSession()`, which is `requireSession()`, and that throws `unauthorized()` when the session is null. `withRouteErrorHandling` turns that `AppError` into a 401.

Why the others are wrong:
- *500*: the parse error is caught inside `readSession`.
- *403*: there is no session to check a role on.
- *400*: the body is never reached; the session check comes first.

excerpts.quote: try { return JSON.parse(raw) as SessionUser; } catch { return null; }

notes.title: Reading before the transaction: last write wins
notes.body:
**Key: both succeed, the last write wins, and both rows record a stale fromAssigneeId.**

`reassignTicket` loads the ticket with `requireWorkflowTicket` (line 791) *before* opening `prisma.$transaction` (line 793), and `updateTicket` updates by id alone. Both leads read the same current assignee. Both transactions then write their new assignee; the second simply overwrites the first. Each writes an `AssignmentHistory` row whose "from" is the assignee they read, so both say "from" the same old person, and the history does not chain.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The second blocks on a row lock*: the read happens outside the transaction and takes no lock.
- *One rolls back*: nothing compares versions, so neither fails.
- *Serialization error*: Prisma uses the database default, READ COMMITTED, which does not raise one here.

excerpts.quote: const ticket = await requireWorkflowTicket(ticketId); const updated = await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
two leads reassigning at once both succeed, the last write wins, and both `AssignmentHistory` rows record the same stale `fromAssigneeId`.

notes.title: Closed tickets take no more notes
notes.body:
**Key: 409, because closed tickets must be reopened before internal work continues.**

`addInternalNote` first runs `assertCanAddInternalNote`, which an agent passes. It then loads the ticket and checks `ticket.status === "CLOSED"`, throwing `conflict("Closed tickets must be reopened before internal work continues.")` before the transaction that would write the note.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Adds the note*: the CLOSED check applies to notes as well as replies.
- *403 for leads and managers*: no role-based exception exists here; the refusal is a 409 for everyone.
- *Reopens automatically*: nothing changes the status in this function.

excerpts.quote: if (ticket.status === "CLOSED") { throw conflict("Closed tickets must be reopened before internal work continues.");

notes.title: The table speaks before the closed-ticket rule
notes.body:
**Key: "Tickets cannot move directly from CLOSED to PENDING."**

`changeTicketStatus` runs `assertCanChangeStatus` (an agent passes), loads the ticket, and then calls `assertValidStatusTransition(ticket.status, input.status)`. In `allowedTransitions`, `CLOSED` lists only `OPEN`, so it throws `conflict(`Tickets cannot move directly from ${current} to ${next}.`)`. The closed-ticket check on the following lines is never reached.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Closed tickets must reopen to OPEN*: that check comes after the table and only fires for moves the table allows.
- *Allowed*: the table has no CLOSED to PENDING edge.
- *This role cannot change ticket workflow status*: agents pass `canModifyTickets`.

excerpts.quote: RESOLVED: ["OPEN", "CLOSED", "ESCALATED"], CLOSED: ["OPEN"],
